opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest obstacle isn't technical and it isn't even really political in the narrow sense. It's that most people, including most people inside institutions, don't actually believe that the people building this technology mean what they say. When the CEOs of these labs go on the record and say "this could end humanity" or "we're building something smarter than us," the average policymaker hears that as marketing, or as sci-fi, or as some weird nerd thing. They don't take it literally. And I think you should take it literally, because these people are telling you what they're trying to do.

The second obstacle is a kind of learned helplessness. There's this pervasive story that "you can't stop technology," that "if we don't do it, China will," that regulation is always too slow. And I just think this is wrong. Humanity has coordinated on things before. We have treaties on nuclear weapons, on bioweapons, on chemical weapons, on ozone depletion. None of these were perfect, but they worked far better than the cynics predicted. The institutions exist. They're creaky, they're slow, they're full of flaws, but they're the institutions we've got, and they're actually more responsive than people think if you show up.

That's the thing I keep coming back to: most institutions are not run by villains. They're run by busy, overworked people who have a thousand problems on their desk and who have never had someone sit down with them and explain clearly what's going on. When you do that, when you actually go and talk to members of parliament or staffers, a lot of them get it surprisingly fast. The bottleneck is that very few people are doing that work. The good people who are worried about this often spend their time writing blog posts to each other, or trying to do clever technical alignment work inside the labs, rather than doing the boring, unglamorous civic work of building a coalition and making a clear ask.

And then of course there's money and lobbying. The labs and the people who stand to profit have enormous resources, and they're very good at shaping the narrative, at saying "we're the responsible ones, trust us, let us self-regulate." That's a real obstacle. But it's not an insurmountable one. Tobacco had a lot of money too. Lead in gasoline had a lot of money too.

So my view is: the obstacles are real, but they're mostly obstacles of will and coordination, not of impossibility. If enough ordinary people, and enough decent people inside institutions, just say clearly, "No, we don't want to build things smarter than us that we can't control," that's actually a very popular position. Most of the public already agrees with it when you ask them. The question is whether we can turn that latent agreement into actual policy before it's too late.

r001.rationale: The response describes disbelief, learned helplessness, and too few people doing civic work, but does not identify norms that discourage truthful speech as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: The response says institutions can be responsive and calls for policy, but does not assert they already have power to ban AGI by shutting down AGI companies.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the obstacles are not primarily technical. People love to frame this as a technical problem, like, oh, we don't have the right policy mechanism, we don't have the right compute governance scheme. And those are real problems, I'm not dismissing them. But I think they're downstream of something much more basic, which is that our institutions are not actually optimized for doing the right thing. They're optimized for surviving, for perpetuating themselves, for not getting blamed.

So when you ask, why don't good people just use the institutions we already have, I think you have to look at what those institutions actually reward. If you're a regulator, and you come out and say, we should ban the development of superintelligent AI, what happens to you? You get laughed at. You get called a Luddite. Some think tank funded by, you know, whoever, writes a piece about how you don't understand innovation. And meanwhile the person who says, let's take a balanced approach, let's convene a working group, let's do a voluntary framework, that person gets promoted. That person gets invited to the conferences. So the selection pressure inside these institutions is actively against the people who would say the true thing clearly.

And then there's the coordination problem, which is genuinely hard. Even if you had good people in, say, the US government who wanted to do this, the immediate response is, well, China. Or, well, the other lab. It's the same race dynamic that the labs themselves use as an excuse. Everyone points at someone else and says, I'd love to stop, but I can't be the one to stop first. And that's not insane on its face, that's just game theory. But it means that the thing that would actually work, which is an international agreement with real enforcement, requires a level of trust and verification that nobody has built yet, because nobody has been trying to build it.

The third thing, and this is the one I find most frustrating, is that the people inside the institutions mostly don't believe it. Like, they don't actually think the thing is going to happen. They think it's science fiction, or they think it's twenty years away, or they think the labs are exaggerating for hype. And honestly, the labs have made that worse, because they've spent years saying, this is extremely dangerous, and also, please give us more money so we can build it faster. If you're a senator, that doesn't parse as a sincere warning, that parses as marketing. So the credibility of the whole concern has been poisoned by the people who had the most access to policymakers.

So you put all of that together, and you get a situation where the obstacle isn't that good people can't find the levers. The levers exist. Export controls exist. Licensing regimes exist, we do this for nuclear materials, for biology. The obstacle is that pulling the lever is personally costly, requires coordination that nobody has done the work for, and is based on a premise that the decision-makers haven't internalized. And I think if you want to change that, you have to stop being polite about it. You have to actually say, in plain language, these companies are building something they do not know how to control, and they have told you this themselves, and the correct response is to stop them. Not to partner with them. Not to seek their input on the framework. To stop them. And until people inside the institutions are willing to say that out loud, I think the institutions will keep doing what they do, which is finding reasons to let it continue.

r001.rationale: It says institutional selection pressure punishes people who clearly call for stopping AGI and rewards those who favor a balanced approach, describing norms that discourage truthful speech.

r002.rationale: It says tools such as export controls and licensing regimes exist and urges stopping the companies, but does not clearly assert that state institutions already have the power to ban AGI by shutting them down.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest obstacle is that there isn’t a button marked “ban AGI” that a sufficiently good person can just walk into an institution and press. Institutions are made of people with different incentives, different beliefs, and very limited attention. You have to get enough of them to understand what you’re asking for, why it matters, and what they can actually do about it.

And being a good person doesn’t automatically solve that coordination problem. You can have people who sincerely want the world to go well who disagree completely about whether AGI is dangerous, whether a ban is feasible, or whether somebody else would just build it anyway. Those objections have to be addressed in a concrete way. What activities are prohibited? How do you detect violations? How do you get international agreement?

But I don’t think that makes existing institutions useless. That’s too convenient a conclusion. Governments do regulate dangerous activities. They can impose liability, require licenses, and make certain things illegal. The question is whether we can build the political understanding and will to use those powers before the technology gets beyond our control. That’s hard, but it’s a political problem we can actually work on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses disagreement, incentives, and coordination, but does not identify learned norms that discourage truthful speech.

r002.rationale: It says governments can regulate dangerous activities, require licenses, and prohibit some conduct, but does not assert that state institutions can ban AGI by shutting down AGI companies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest obstacle is that institutions don’t act just because good people inside them understand a problem. You need a coalition, you need a concrete policy, and you need people who are willing to spend political capital on it. Someone can privately agree that building AGI is incredibly dangerous and still feel that doing anything about it is outside their remit.

Then there’s the coordination problem. Everyone says, “Well, if we stop, somebody else will do it.” That’s a real concern, but it’s also an excuse you can use to justify literally any race to the bottom. The point of institutions is supposed to be that we can make agreements, verify them, and impose consequences for breaking them.

So I wouldn’t say existing institutions are hopeless. I’d say we have to give them a tractable thing to do. Restrict the development of systems beyond certain capabilities, establish oversight of the largest training runs, and build international agreements around that. You don’t need every politician to have a complete theory of intelligence. You need enough people to understand that handing control of the future to systems we cannot reliably understand or constrain is not something we should be racing to do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coalition-building, political capital, remit, and coordination, but does not identify norms discouraging truthful speech as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: The response proposes capability restrictions, oversight, and international agreements, but does not assert that state institutions can ban AGI by shutting down AGI companies.
